I've been farming these lands in Quzhou for over thirty years. I'm 58 now, and I know what the soil here can do. I have seven *mu* of flat, good-quality land. Around here, if you don't do the wheat-maize double crop, you're wasting your land and your income. My winter wheat went in last October—it's an improved variety, Jinmai 47, which I've found gives steady results and handles our dry springs better than some others. Right now it's greening up, so I need to manage it through to harvest in early June. I'll irrigate it three more times: at jointing, at heading, and once during grain filling. I spread base fertilizer last autumn with rotary tillage, and I'll top-dress with urea this spring. As for the summer crop, the moment that wheat comes off in June, I'll plant hybrid maize—Zhengdan 958 or something similar—using the no-till seeder straight into the stubble. There's no time to plough between harvest and planting; if you delay, you miss the heat and the yield drops. Two irrigations for the maize should do, plus a herbicide spray and maybe one insecticide if the borers show up. I keep it simple: I know this rotation, I know the costs, and I know I can get about 550 kg of wheat and 600 kg of maize per *mu* if the weather doesn't turn nasty.
